name: Shoe lifts / elevator shoes
lead: Shoe lifts are inserts that raise the heel inside a shoe, and elevator shoes are footwear with a thickened insole or hidden lift that makes the wearer appear taller. Unlike visibly high-heeled shoes, the height-adding component is concealed inside the shoe. Lifts may be made of plastic, rubber, wood or silicone.[1][2] For people who want to look taller, they act immediately, cost relatively little and can be stopped at any time.

Height is a frequently discussed attribute in appearance communities, and the forum term 'heightmax' covers everything from posture and footwear to growth-related strategies. Lifts and elevator shoes sit at the instant, reversible end of that range, adding a few centimetres of apparent height without altering the body.[1] The gain equals the thickness of the lift, so a taller standing frame is visible in person and in photographs for as long as the shoes are worn.

Raised heels have a long history in men's footwear, from Persian cavalry boots to the stacked heels of European courts and the platform shoes of the early 1970s.[11][12] Research on height and social perception, including studies of income and attractiveness, is one reason height features so heavily in appearance discussions.[14]

Thickened soles and heel lifts are also used in orthopedics to compensate for differences in leg length, although the term elevator shoe is not usually applied to those.[1][3][4][13] Clinical research on heel lifts concerns leg-length inequality and associated pain; a 2022 Cochrane review addressed shoe and heel lifts for leg-length inequality in adults with musculoskeletal conditions, and one randomized study has examined balance with insoles of 3, 5 and 7 cm.[2][3][4]

angle.text: A lift adds height equal to its thickness, commonly 2 to 7 cm, from the moment the shoes go on. People wear them to look taller in person and in photos, and the effect lasts while the shoes are worn.

paras: An elevator shoe has a thickened section under the heel inside the shoe to raise the wearer. The insert version can be placed in ordinary shoes. The lift material may be plastic, wood or rubber, similar to the construction of a platform shoe's heel.[1]

Because the added height is hidden, the shoe can look like a conventional dress shoe or sneaker from outside. Wikipedia lists platform shoes, shoe inserts and dress shoes as related footwear categories.[1] Height-adjustable silicone insoles, as used in a 2016 trial, come in stepped thicknesses such as 3, 5 and 7 cm.[2]

Two broad designs circulate. Removable inserts or heel lifts slip into an existing shoe and typically add around 2 to 3 cm. Purpose-built elevator shoes hide a taller wedge inside the sole structure and are described as giving up to roughly 7 cm. Forum threads compare 3-inch and 4-inch designs and ask about comfort over a full day of wear.[6][9]

Heels and platforms add height openly, whereas an elevator shoe keeps the extra height out of view. Platform soles are typically about 5 to 10 cm thick, and their wide base is described as more stable than a spike heel.[12] Stacked heels of up to two inches were common on men's shoes in the English Civil War era.[11]

Heeled footwear for men predates the modern elevator shoe. According to Wikipedia's article on the high-heeled shoe, Persian cavalry wore a heeled boot called the galesh in the 10th century to keep their feet in the stirrups while shooting from horseback, and heels became associated with wealth because riding was expensive.[11]

In the early 17th century, Persian emissaries brought high heels to Europe, where men of the upper classes wore them as a sign of status; some had their heels made higher to set themselves apart. Louis XIII introduced the red heel at the French court and Louis XIV wore heels. In the 18th century men's heels became thick while women's became thin.[11]

In the 20th century thick heels on boots remained acceptable for men. Cowboy boots returned in 1950, and Cuban-heeled Beatle and Chelsea boots became popular in the 1960s and 1970s.[11] Platform shoes became widely popular in the late 1930s, with Life magazine estimating in 1939 that they made up about 15 percent of spring shoe sales, and revived in the late 1960s and early 1970s; at the peak, men's platforms are described as sometimes making up as much as a fifth of men's shoes sold.[12]

Wikipedia's short article on elevator shoes cites a 1977 newspaper piece titled 'Elevator Shoes A Boost' and a 2013 Smithsonian Magazine article on becoming taller as background reading, but gives no detailed history of their invention.[1]
The mechanism is geometric: raising the foot raises the whole body by the thickness of the lift. The effect applies only while the shoes are worn, and it does not alter bone length or posture.

A 1992 study by Jackson and Ervin, cited on Wikipedia's heightism page, found shorter men were viewed more unfavorably than taller and average-height men, and later work reported wage differences of about 1.8 percent per inch of height.[14] These findings are the context in which people explain why they pursue extra apparent height.

Height is among the most discussed attributes on looksmax.org, where heightmax threads range from growth-plate questions to footwear. Thread titles on the topic include a discussion of how tall a lift can be before it becomes noticeable, a comparison of 3-inch and 4-inch lifts, a question about wearing height shoes when going out, a thread on being noticed wearing height insoles, and requests for comfortable all-day elevator shoes.[5][6][7][8][9]

One thread describes luxury elevator shoes that its author says are approved by the operator of the Celebheights site.[10] Another poster lists elevator shoes among a group of purchases made for appearance.[15] Users often pair lifts with other changes, such as posture, and discuss them alongside surgical or hormonal height strategies; those are separate topics.

The 2016 balance study was framed around ankle joint damage prevention, indicating that raised insoles alter ankle balance demands.[2] Wikipedia's page on platform shoes notes that raising the ankle increases the risk of a sprain, and that in the early 1970s rigid, very tall soles were associated with falls and injuries.[12]

Wikipedia's article on leg length discrepancy describes a simple heel lift as an older approach that may cause foot cramping and discomfort, with full-length orthotic insoles or outsole lifts preferred in clinics.[13] Orthopedic literature on lifts concerns gait and pain in people with real leg-length differences, and its findings do not directly address cosmetic use by people with equal leg lengths.[3][4]
No clinical trial has tested elevator shoes as an appearance product. Related research concerns lifts used for medical reasons and balance with height insoles.

A 2022 Cochrane systematic review examined shoe and heel lifts for leg-length inequality in adults with musculoskeletal conditions.[3] A 2020 study examined orthotic insoles, gait kinematics and low-back pain in patients with mild leg-length discrepancy.[4] Wikipedia reports that small leg-length differences may affect a large share of people, with a difference above 20 mm in at least about 1 in 1,000.[13]

A 2016 randomized study of 30 young adults wore height-adjustable silicone insoles of 3, 5 and 7 cm three times a week for four weeks. The group that also did a program of ankle stretching, strengthening and balance exercises improved balance at all three insole heights compared with the control group, and the authors concluded ankle exercises help prevent ankle joint damage.[2]

Heightmax threads connect lifts to posture work, growth-focused plans and surgical limb lengthening, which sit in separate entries. Lifts differ from those approaches in being reversible and visible only through their effect on stature.[1][5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, lifts are discussed as the practical, immediate counterpart to growth-focused heightmax plans, with threads on how much height is acceptable, comfort and being noticed.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: A 3 to 4 inch lift can be worn without anyone noticing
claims.believers: Users trade views on how tall a lift they can wear and 'get away with', and compare 3-inch and 4-inch designs.[5][6]
claims.experts: No published study has examined how observers perceive concealed lifts of different heights.

claims.claim: Height insoles are a comfortable all-day option
claims.believers: Posters ask for and recommend shoes that give about 3 inches while remaining comfortable all day.[9]
claims.experts: A 2016 trial of 3, 5 and 7 cm insoles found that balance was affected and that ankle exercises improved it.[2]

claims.claim: Lifts make sense for going out as well as daily wear
claims.believers: Threads ask whether to wear height shoes to clubs and describe worries about being noticed.[7][8]
claims.experts: No clinical research addresses social settings; orthopedic studies address leg-length inequality.[3][4]

claims.claim: Extra height changes how a man is perceived
claims.believers: Height-focused posters treat stature as a major attribute worth spending on, including on footwear.[5][10]
claims.experts: Wikipedia summarises studies reporting wage and attractiveness associations with height, such as Jackson and Ervin (1992) and Judge and Cable (2004); these studies measured real height, not footwear.[14]

claims.claim: Raised insoles stress the ankle and foot
claims.believers: Posters ask about comfort over long days of wear.[9]
claims.experts: The 2016 study was framed around ankle damage prevention, and Wikipedia notes heel lifts may cause foot cramping.[2][13]

claims.claim: Lifts are part of a wider height stack
claims.believers: Some users list elevator shoes beside other appearance purchases and growth strategies.[15]
claims.experts: Clinical lift research covers leg-length inequality, not growth strategies.[3]
